newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTERVIEW-Sanlam cheers S.African govt discipline.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sanlam cheers S.African govt discipline.

text.p: South Africa has proved its commitment to fiscal discipline, but the economic growth the government's policies will generate is unlikely to occur before 1999, Sanlam chairman Marinus Daling said in an interview.

Daling told Reuters he was impressed by the three-year-old government's implementation of the macroeconomic policies in Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's June 1996 programme for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR.

He said Manuel's March 12 budget, including a four percent deficit target and renewed commitment to the privatisation of state assets, had demonstrated a commitment to creating the conditions for higher growth and job creation.

"I believe those are two strong signals that the government intends to stay with GEAR. The emphasis should now be on the implementation of GEAR and I am quite satisfied with what I have seen up to now," he said.
Daling, one of a panel of white businessmen who have advised President Nelson Mandela on economic and other issues, heads the country's second biggest investment company.

Though the mutual company is divesting itself of controlling holdings in industrial companies and moving towards a concentration on financial services, Sanlam remains one of the "big five" dominating control of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

Daling said Manuel's policies and central Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals' taught monetary policy were creating confidence in South Africa, but he said winning over foreign investors would take longer.
"We have to realise that we are competing for the investment rand with the other emerging markets...we have some way to go to get higher up that league table," he said.
Daling said he expected a reduction in the Reserve Bank's 17 percent official Bank rate late in the year or early next year.
"I would hope that we would see lower interest rates towards the end of this year and the beginning of next year.

"I would think we could have a consistent trend towards lower interest rates. If you look at our real rates of interest, we are out of line with the most of the developed world and the developing world," he said.

In a separate interview, Sanlam chief economist Jac Laubscher said he expected two reductions of one percentage point each before the end of the year, but did not expect the rate to drop below 15 percent.

He predicted inflation would fall from the current 9.6 percent in March to a low of seven percent in the first half of 1998, but not further, leaving real interest rates around their current level of seven to eight percent.
Daling said he believed the government was creating the conditions for economic growth to accelerate beyond the 1996 level of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product.
"I would expect our economy to grow faster...I think that we can achieve five percent, but I don't think that it will be this year or next year," he said.
Daling was more optimistic than the 16 economists polled in a Reuter consensus forecast, who predicted growth in 1999 of between 2.3 percent and 4.5 percent, with a mean forecast of 3.7 percent.
Daling cited escalating crime and the flight of white skills as two trends threatening South Africa's recovery since white rule ended with Mandela's April 1994 election.
A massive post-apartheid escalation in serious crimes including murder, rape, assault and vehicle hijacking has resisted government efforts to impose law and order.

"I think crime is an impediment to any form of investment. To some extent, it is a result of our past and moving from an authoritarian society into a democratic society, but I think it is important that we act against crime," Daling said.

"I personally believe that the flight of skills from South Africa is one of the most serious situations in our community. We need skills to train new skills. If we lose our existing skills base some people believe it will create a skill vacuum for people to step into, but the world doesn't work like that."
He said fears for the quality of education and health care and affirmative action policies targeting blacks were the major causes.
